ACIAR Monograph 143, published by the Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research (ACIAR) in partnership with NSW Department of Primary Industries, the Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI), Murdoch University, University of Canberra, and MAFF, under ACIAR Project ASEM/2000/109. text:
Corn is generally ready for harvest once it reaches physiological maturity, indicated by husks turning dry and brown, the "milk line" on the kernel having disappeared, and a dark abscission ("black") layer having formed at the base of the kernel (see the grain-fill and maturity growth-stage topic for how these indicators develop). Grain moisture at physiological maturity is still fairly high -- farmers in this source's account are described harvesting anywhere from roughly 24-28% moisture (for further drying) down to 14-15% moisture (suitable for more direct storage), depending on their drying setup and market.

Harvesting at the right time matters for reducing field losses from birds, insects, mould, and weather damage -- leaving mature grain standing in wet conditions raises the risk of aflatoxin contamination (see the aflatoxin disease topic).
